blocks.text: A 19-year-old university student is admitted with meningococcal meningitis for the second time in two years. Tests of antibody levels and white cell counts are normal, but the haemolytic complement assay (CH50) is almost zero. One missing protein in a cascade of about thirty explains why the same bacterium keeps getting through.

blocks.markdown: Complement is a set of about 30 plasma and membrane proteins, mostly made in the liver, that circulate as inactive precursors. Activation proceeds as a **proteolytic cascade**: each activated enzyme cleaves the next component, so one initiating event is amplified enormously. Three pathways differ only in how they begin; all converge on cleavage of **C3**, and then share the same three outputs: opsonisation, inflammation and lysis.

blocks.title: Complement cascade
blocks.text: A series of plasma proteins that are sequentially cleaved and activated on microbial surfaces. Cleavage yields a small soluble fragment (named 'a') and a larger fragment (named 'b') that usually binds the target surface and forms the next enzyme.

rows: Antibody (IgG or IgM) bound to antigen; C-reactive protein on microbes
C1q, C1r, C1s, then C4 and C2
Mannose-containing carbohydrates on microbial surfaces, recognised by mannose-binding lectin (MBL) or ficolins
MBL/ficolin with MASP-1 and MASP-2, then C4 and C2
Spontaneous slow hydrolysis ('tick-over') of C3 and binding of C3b to surfaces that lack regulators; no antibody needed
C3, factor B, factor D; stabilised by properdin
blocks.caption: The three activation pathways

blocks.markdown: **Classical** activation needs antibody, so it bridges adaptive and innate immunity; C1q binds the Fc regions of antibody (IgM best, then IgG) clustered on an antigen. The **lectin** pathway acts like the classical pathway but is triggered by carbohydrate patterns, and so works before antibody exists. The **alternative** pathway is always ticking over at a low rate: C3b formed by hydrolysis lands on any nearby surface. On healthy host cells it is rapidly inactivated by regulators (factor H, factor I, DAF/CD55, CD46), but on a microbe with no regulators it is stabilised and amplifies. Because C3b generates more C3 convertase, the alternative pathway also acts as an **amplification loop** for the other two.

blocks.title: Which pathway first?
blocks.prompt: A neonate (no antibody of its own beyond maternal IgG) has yeast cells with mannose-rich walls in the bloodstream. Which complement pathway is most likely to start the response, and which enzyme then cleaves C3?

steps.text: Ask whether antibody is needed. The neonate has not yet made specific antibody, so a pathway that requires antibody binding (classical) is unlikely to be the first.

Look at the target. Mannose-rich carbohydrates are recognised by mannose-binding lectin, so the lectin pathway is a good candidate; the alternative pathway also operates on unprotected surfaces and amplifies.
Follow the lectin pathway. MBL bound to the yeast activates MASP-1 and MASP-2, which cleave C4 and C2 to form the C3 convertase C4b2a.
C4b2a cleaves many C3 molecules into C3a and C3b; the C3b coats the yeast (opsonisation) and feeds the alternative amplification loop.

blocks.answer: The lectin pathway, with C4b2a as the C3 convertase, supported by alternative-pathway amplification.

blocks.markdown: **The three outputs.** (1) **C3b** is the principal **opsonin**: it coats microbes and is recognised by complement receptors (CR1, CR3) on phagocytes. (2) **C3a and C5a** are **anaphylatoxins**: they bind receptors on mast cells and other cells to cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability; C5a is also a powerful **chemoattractant** for neutrophils. C5a is made when a C5 convertase (C3b added to the C3 convertase) cleaves C5. (3) The larger fragment **C5b** nucleates the **membrane attack complex (MAC)**: C5b binds C6, C7 and C8 and recruits multiple C9 molecules (C5b-9) to form a pore in the membrane, causing osmotic lysis. The MAC is especially important for killing Neisseria species, whose thin outer membrane is vulnerable to it. Host cells are protected from the MAC by **CD59** (protectin).

blocks.latex: \text{Number of C3b molecules generated} \approx k \times n \times t
blocks.caption: Simplified amplification model: k = C3 molecules cleaved per convertase per minute, n = convertases present, t = time in minutes

blocks.title: Amplification on a microbial surface
blocks.prompt: In a simplified model each C3 convertase cleaves 120 C3 molecules per minute. If 8 convertases are assembled on a bacterium, estimate the number of C3b molecules produced in 3 minutes, assuming every cleavage gives one C3b and ignoring loss.

steps.text: Identify the model variables: k = 120 per minute, n = 8, t = 3 minutes.
Multiply to obtain the total number of cleavage events.

Interpret: a handful of convertases rapidly deposit thousands of C3b molecules, which is why a few initiating events can fully opsonise a microbe. Real rates differ, and regulators such as factor H limit this on host cells; the number is only to show the scale of amplification.

blocks.answer: About 2880 C3b molecules, illustrating the amplification of the cascade.

rows: Impaired clearance of immune complexes; autoimmune disease resembling systemic lupus erythematosus; some pyogenic infections
Severe, recurrent infections with encapsulated pyogenic bacteria; immune-complex disease
Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis and disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection
Hereditary angioedema: recurrent swelling (not infection); low C4 between and during attacks
Common; usually mild or silent, may modestly raise infection risk in infancy
blocks.caption: Inherited complement deficiencies and what to predict

blocks.title: Match the defect to the job lost
blocks.text: C3 is needed for opsonisation, so its loss means bacterial infections that need phagocytosis. Terminal components make the MAC, which is needed mainly against Neisseria, so their loss gives recurrent meningococcal or gonococcal disease. Early classical components clear immune complexes, so their loss gives autoimmune disease.

items: Three pathways, one convergence on C3.
C3b opsonises; C3a and C5a cause inflammation (C5a recruits neutrophils); C5b-9 forms the MAC.
Regulators (factor H, DAF, CD59) protect host cells.
Deficiencies predict infections: C3 (pyogenic), terminal (Neisseria), early classical (immune complex disease).

points: Classical (antibody, C1q), lectin (MBL on microbial carbohydrate) and alternative (spontaneous C3b on unprotected surfaces) pathways all generate a C3 convertase.
C3b is the opsonin, C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins (C5a also chemotactic) and C5b-9 is the membrane attack complex.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection; early component deficiency to immune complex disease.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway is triggered by antibody bound to antigen?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: C1q binds the Fc region of clustered IgG or IgM.
distractorRationale.b: The lectin pathway is triggered by microbial carbohydrates, not antibody.
distractorRationale.c: The alternative pathway needs no antibody; it starts from C3b on unprotected surfaces.
distractorRationale.d: 'Terminal' refers to the shared final steps, not an activation pathway.

questions.explanation: The classical pathway begins when C1q binds to clustered antibody (IgM or IgG) on an antigen. The lectin and alternative pathways begin without antibody, which lets them act early in a first encounter.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the alternative pathway can start without antibody or lectin?

options.text: C1q binds directly to bacterial DNA
Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 produces C3b that can bind any nearby surface and is stabilised where regulators are absent
Factor H is required for activation

questions.correctOptionText: Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 produces C3b that can bind any nearby surface and is stabilised where regulators are absent

distractorRationale.a: C1q binds antibody and some pattern ligands, not DNA, and it is part of the classical pathway.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: tick-over C3b is deposited on surfaces; on microbes it forms C3bBb and amplifies.
distractorRationale.c: MASP-2 acts in the lectin pathway and cleaves C4 and C2.
distractorRationale.d: Factor H is an inhibitor of the alternative pathway, not an activator.

questions.explanation: The alternative pathway relies on continuous low-level C3 hydrolysis. Surfaces lacking regulators such as factor H allow C3bBb to persist and amplify, whereas host cells destroy it, which is how self and non-self are distinguished.

questions.stem: A researcher selectively blocks C5a receptors on neutrophils in an infection model. Which function is most directly impaired?

options.text: Formation of pores by the membrane attack complex
Chemotactic recruitment of neutrophils to the site

questions.correctOptionText: Chemotactic recruitment of neutrophils to the site

distractorRationale.a: Opsonisation depends on C3b and complement receptors, not C5a receptors.
distractorRationale.b: The MAC is formed by C5b-9 and does not require C5a signalling.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: C5a is a chemoattractant and activator of neutrophils.
distractorRationale.d: Immune complex clearance depends on early classical components and CR1.

questions.explanation: C5a signals through its receptor on neutrophils to attract and activate them. Blocking that receptor leaves opsonisation and MAC formation intact but impairs neutrophil recruitment.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a second episode of disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Which inherited defect is most likely?

options.text: Deficiency of C3 receptor CR3 on lymphocytes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: terminal component deficiency impairs MAC formation, the key defence against Neisseria.
distractorRationale.b: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes angioedema, not Neisserial infection.
distractorRationale.c: CR3 is a phagocyte receptor; it is not the classical association with recurrent Neisseria infection.
distractorRationale.d: IgE deficiency is not associated with this infection pattern.

questions.explanation: The MAC is the major complement-mediated killing mechanism against Neisseria, so deficiency of C5 to C9 leads to recurrent or disseminated Neisseria infection. Other defects predict different patterns.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent severe infections with encapsulated pyogenic bacteria from infancy. Serum C3 is undetectable and CH50 is absent. Which statement best explains the pyogenic infection pattern?

options.text: C3 is needed for opsonisation and for assembly of the C5 convertase, so both phagocytosis and lysis are impaired
C3 deficiency selectively reduces antibody production
C3 deficiency increases opsonisation through C4b

questions.correctOptionText: C3 is needed for opsonisation and for assembly of the C5 convertase, so both phagocytosis and lysis are impaired

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with no C3b, bacteria are not opsonised, and the C5 convertase cannot form.
distractorRationale.b: C3 loss affects opsonisation as well as the lytic pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Antibody production is largely preserved, though immune complex disease may occur.
distractorRationale.d: C4b is not an adequate substitute for C3b opsonisation.

questions.explanation: C3b is the central opsonin, so its absence impairs phagocytosis of encapsulated bacteria; it is also needed for the C5 convertase. This produces severe pyogenic infections and also affects lysis.

questions.stem: True or false: the membrane attack complex is formed from C5b, C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9 molecules.
questions.explanation: The MAC is the C5b-9 complex: C5b, C6, C7, C8 and a ring of several C9 molecules form a transmembrane pore. This is the lytic arm of complement.

questions.stem: In a simplified model each C3 convertase cleaves 200 C3 molecules per minute. A bacterium carries 15 convertases. Assuming each cleavage yields one C3b and ignoring losses, how many C3b molecules are produced in 2 minutes?
questions.explanation: The model is N = k × n × t = 200 × 15 × 2 = 6000. This illustrates why a small number of initiating events can coat a surface with opsonin; in life, regulators and losses reduce the true number.

questions.stem: C7 deficiency is autosomal recessive. Two unaffected carrier parents plan a family. What is the probability, in percent, that a given child is affected?
questions.explanation: Each carrier transmits the deficient allele with probability 1/2, so the child is affected with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, which is 25%. The probability is the same for each child, independent of earlier children.

questions.stem: Compare how the classical and alternative pathways are initiated and state what they share.
markingGuide: Classical: antibody (IgM/IgG) bound to antigen or CRP; C1q then C1r/C1s; cleaves C4 and C2 giving C4b2a
Alternative: spontaneous C3 hydrolysis/tick-over; C3b on surfaces lacking regulators; factor B and factor D give C3bBb stabilised by properdin
Both generate a C3 convertase that cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b
Both lead to C5 convertase and the same terminal pathway, opsonisation and inflammation
questions.explanation: The pathways differ in how they start (antibody versus unprotected surface) but converge on C3 convertase and share the downstream outputs.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent meningococcal infection and a normal C3 level but a very low CH50. Explain the likely defect, the role of the missing step and why C3b-dependent opsonisation is preserved.
markingGuide: Terminal component (C5 to C9) deficiency, so MAC cannot form
The MAC lyses Neisseria, which have thin outer membranes
C3 level normal so C3b opsonisation and C3a/C5a generation (apart from loss of C5 in C5 deficiency) are preserved
CH50 low because it measures total haemolytic activity requiring the full pathway
Infection pattern Neisseria rather than pyogenic encapsulated bacteria
questions.explanation: The MAC is the pathway-specific defence against Neisseria. Normal C3 means opsonisation and the earlier cascade work, so phagocytes still clear most other bacteria.
